However, abortion providers and civil rights advocates challenge the law, arguing that it creates an unconstitutional obstacle for women seeking an abortion. You hear a car backfire and your body reacts before your brain can catch up. It makes you quiet. It makes you distant, sometimes even from the people who love you the most. But it also gives you a profound gratitude for the quiet moments, for every single day you get to breathe normal air. You carry the weight of the friends you lost, and that stays with you every second of every day.

You know, you don't come back from a place like that the same person you were when you left. It changes how you look at everything, from the small daily frustrations that used to bother you to how you view the world at large. You carry the weight of the friends you lost, and that stays with you every single day. But it also gives you a profound appreciation for life and for the people around you. You realize how fragile things are, and you try not to sweat the small stuff anymore because you've seen what real hardship looks like. It's a continuous process of readjusting, trying to integrate those experiences into who you are now without letting them define every single part of your future.

Well, you know, when you think about soldiers coming back from a place like Iraq, it reminds me a lot of what happened to the guys coming home from Vietnam. They're dropped into these terrible, high-stakes situations where they have to survive, and then suddenly they're expected to just step back into normal life like nothing happened. But you can't unsee that kind of hardship. It changes how you look at the world, how you look at your own safety and your family. And just like those stories my family used to tell about surviving the South or the hard times in Watts, these veterans are carrying heavy things, and they're going to have to find a way to live with it, with a smile on their lips or not.

Definitely. Serving here and working side-by-side with the Iraqi army and living out in these communities really strips away a lot of the abstractions you might have coming into it. You see people just trying to live their lives, raise their families, and get through the day, much like anyone back home. It gives you a deep appreciation for the common humanity in folks, even across vast cultural and linguistic divides. You realize that most people everywhere just want peace, stability, and a fair chance at a future. It's changed how I view not just the people here, but people in general—it makes you much more patient and much more willing to listen to someone else's story before making any judgments.

It really has. When you spend months living side-by-side with Iraqi soldiers, sharing the same risks, seeing them work through their own challenges and trying to secure their neighborhoods, it strips away a lot of the abstract notions you might have had before deploying. You stop seeing a whole population through the lens of just headlines or sectarian conflict. You start seeing individual people who want the exact same things we do: safety for their families, a chance to do their jobs, and a future where they don't have to worry about violence in the streets. Working closely with them, and seeing the dedication of the guys in my own unit day in and day out, changes how you view resilience and human nature. You realize people are remarkably adaptable and generally want to build rather than destroy, given half a chance.

It really has. You go through something like that, where everything you thought was permanent gets stripped away, and you suddenly realize how thin the line is between all of us. Before, I think I was moving through life in my own bubble, not really paying attention to the quiet struggles happening right next to me on the street or even within my own neighborhood. But when you hit rock bottom, you see the pure kindness of strangers, people with nothing to give who still share what they have. It humbles you completely. It makes you understand that we are all carrying some kind of heavy weight, and the only way we get through any of this is by looking out for one another with a lot more grace and a lot less judgment.

It really has. When you spend that kind of time overseas and see people living in completely different circumstances, struggling with the exact same fundamental human desires—safety, family, a better future—it strips away a lot of the superficial differences we get caught up in here at home. You realize that most of us just want to live in peace and take care of the people we love. It makes you a lot more patient and a lot less willing to judge someone based on a label or a headline. You start looking at individuals rather than groups, and that changes everything about how you interact with your neighbors.

Well, you know, when you write about people who are pushed to the margins—people who don't usually get to be the center of a story—you start to realize that everybody has an interior life that's just as complex and difficult as your own. Growing up in Watts, surrounded by folks who came up from the South with nothing but hard stories and a smile, you learn pretty quick that life isn't split into simple heroes and villains. You see a guy making an impossible choice between his wife and his mother during a flood, and you understand the weight of humanity. Writing all these books, all these different characters over the years, it just keeps reminding me that we're all carrying around our own histories, trying to make it through the day and protect the people we love.

There is definitely a sense of separation when you return. You spend fifteen months immersed in a very high-stakes environment with a close-knit group of soldiers, experiencing things that are completely outside the everyday reality of most Americans. When you come back to the States, life goes on as normal for everyone else—people are worried about traffic or the latest pop culture news—while you’re still carrying these intense memories and the bond you had with your unit. It can be hard to bridge that gap and explain what it was actually like over there. That is a big part of why sharing our stories and trying to bridge that understanding is so important, because that isolation is a very real challenge for a lot of returning veterans.

You definitely feel that disconnect. When you return, you realize how much of a bubble normal life in America is. You go from an environment every day where your life and the lives of the guys around you are constantly on the line, where everything has immediate, heavy consequences, and you step back into a grocery store where people are stressing out over what kind of cereal to buy. It is jarring. You want to talk about things that happened or explain what you experienced, but you quickly realize most people have no frame of reference for it, and you don't want to burden them or sound like you're complaining. That is a real source of isolation for a lot of returning soldiers, and it takes time to bridge that gap and adjust back to the rhythm of everyday civilian life.

Yeah, absolutely. You come back and people are worried about gas prices or what is happening on reality television, and you just spent a year dodging IEDs and losing friends. You try to explain it, but the look in their eyes tells you they just don't have the frame of reference for it. It is like speaking a different language. You are sitting at a family dinner, everything looks normal on the surface, but inside you feel completely untethered. You realize pretty quickly that the person who left for deployment is not the same person who came back, and the world at home kept spinning without you. That gap can feel impossible to bridge sometimes, so you just keep it to yourself, and that is where the real isolation sets in.

Yeah, absolutely. You come back and you realize right away that the people around you have no frame of reference for what you just spent the last year doing. You're sitting in a restaurant or driving down the highway, and everybody is stressing about things that just feel completely trivial compared to what you were dealing with overseas. It’s hard to talk about it because you don't want to sound dramatic, but you also know that if you try to explain it, they’re just going to look at you with this blank stare or pity, and neither of those helps. So you keep most of it to yourself, and that’s where that gap comes in. You're physically home, but a part of you still feels like you're on a completely different planet from everyone else.

Well, you know, I think that kind of isolation is something that happens whenever people go through an intense, defining experience that the rest of society just watches on a screen or doesn't see at all. For me, it's not war, but it's the simple act of writing every day, of living in the worlds I create and carrying those stories around in my head. When you spend your life immersed in the realities of people who are marginalized, people whose histories aren't being told, you come back to normal, everyday conversation and it feels a little strange. You realize that most folks are walking around blind to the struggles and the richness happening right in their own backyard. That creates a gap. But you bridge it the best way you can—by telling the story.

One image that will always stay with me is from a patrol in late 2008, after the security situation had really started to turn around. We were walking through a neighborhood in southern Baghdad that, just a year earlier, was completely dead, boarded up, and torn apart by sectarian violence. But on this particular afternoon, children were running alongside our patrol, and local shopkeepers were actually out sweeping their entryways and waving at us. It was a simple, quiet moment, but it represented such a profound shift from my first tour in 2006. Seeing that normalcy finally returning to the streets—seeing people daring to hope and live their daily lives again—is something I will carry with me for the rest of my life.

One moment that really sticks with me involves working side-by-side with the Iraqi army troops we were partnered with. There was a specific joint patrol in Baghdad where things could have easily gone sideways, given how volatile things had been just a couple of years prior. But I watched the Iraqi battalion officers execute their staff processes and lead the operation with a level of competence and calm that completely validated the progress we had been seeing. Seeing them take genuine ownership of their city's security—knowing where things stood before compared to the height of the sectarian violence—was a powerful realization. It was the moment I truly felt that the hard work, the long days, and the sacrifice were translating into something sustainable for the future.

I think the image that will stay with me until the day I die is the sheer look of disbelief on people's faces as they wandered through the dust and the ruins. You see these things on a screen, you read about them in the headlines, but seeing the human scale of it up close—the way a person just stands there staring at where their home or their workplace used to be, clutching a single photograph or a pet carrier—that strips away all the politics and statistics. It is just raw, quiet grief. In that moment, you realize how fragile everything we build really is, and yet, right alongside that devastation, you saw neighbors reaching out hands to absolute strangers. That contrast between our capacity for total destruction and our instinct for profound grace is something I will never, ever forget.

There was a moment when we were out on patrol in Baghdad, and we walked past this small schoolyard. The kids were playing soccer with a deflated ball in the dust, and despite everything going on around them, the noise, the tension, the sheer destruction of the city, they were just laughing. One of them looked right at me and waved, a real, genuine kid's smile. It just hit me so hard because it cut through all the politics and the violence and everything else. It reminded me of what normal life looks like, and how fragile it is. That image of those kids playing in the middle of a war zone is something that is just permanently etched in my brain, and I don't think I'll ever be able to shake it.

Well, you know, my mind often goes back to my grandfather sitting on that porch in Watts. He was the only black man in the neighborhood who could read and write, and people would come to him with their letters, their government forms, instructions for a piece of machinery they'd ordered, paying him ten or fifteen cents for his help. And my father would sit quietly in the corner, watching him, absorbing the lesson that reading is the most important thing a person can do. That image of my grandfather on the porch, serving his community just by virtue of literacy and a willingness to help, is something that has stayed with me my entire life. It shaped how I view stories, how I view people, and the dignity in everyday lives that might otherwise go completely unrecorded.

Not anymore. When this deployment wraps up and we finally make it home this spring, I'm really looking forward to turning the page and moving into a new chapter. I've found a real passion for writing and storytelling through my experiences here, collecting the thoughts and perspectives of the soldiers around me. I've given a lot to the Army over these tours, but I'm ready for what's next.

Not really, no. Look, I’m proud of the time I served and the people I served alongside, but that chapter of my life is done. When you are out there, you miss the camaraderie and the sense of purpose, but you also miss a lot of normal life. My family sacrificed a lot while I was deployed, and it is time for me to be there for them fully. The military is a young person's game, and I gave it everything I had. Now it is time to take what I learned and apply it to the civilian world, figure out what's next, and build something new.

Not really. Look, I served my time, and I'm proud of every minute of it, especially the time I spent with the guys downrange. But that chapter of my life is closed. War changes you, and it changes your perspective on what family and the future mean. When you walk away, you realize how much you’ve missed and how much your loved ones have sacrificed while you were gone. My duty now is to them, and to telling the stories of the soldiers who are still over there, making sure the country understands the reality of what they go through every single day. I left the uniform behind, but I’ll never leave that brotherhood.

No, not at all. Writing is what I do. I mean, I have all these things in my head, and I'm continually writing them, three hours a day, 365 days a year. If you want to get rich, you go into real estate. I'm a writer. I've published over 50 books because I just have to keep going, telling the stories of the people and the lives I saw around me.
